entries.520328c1b39004d7614fc1353569383b9fb028fe: <div sID="gen19875" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Hos.10" sID="Hos.10"/> <div eID="gen19875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19876" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19877" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The people of Israel are charged with gross corruptions in the worship of God and are threatened with the destruction of their images and altars, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1-Hos.10.2 Hos.10.5 Hos.10.6 Hos.10.8">ver. 1, 2, 5, 6, 8</reference>. II. They are charged with corruptions in the administration of the civil government and are threatened with the ruin of that, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.3-Hos.10.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.7">7</reference>. III. They are charged with imitating the sins of their fathers, and with security in their own sins, and are threatened with smarting humbling judgments, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.9-Hos.10.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. IV. They are earnestly invited to repent and reform, and are threatened with ruin if they did not, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12-Hos.10.15">ver. 12-15</reference>.
entries.436cc283b5bd1cb0aa863e3a1a27d548217409d5: <div eID="gen19877" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19876" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Degeneracy of Israel; Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 730.)</title> <div sID="gen19878" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Israel <hi type="italic">is</hi> an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images. <hi type="super">2</hi> Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty: he shall break down their altars, he shall spoil their images. <hi type="super">3</hi> For now they shall say, We have no king, because we feared not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; what then should a king do to us? <hi type="super">4</hi> They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field. <hi type="super">5</hi> The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Beth-aven: for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof <hi type="italic">that</hi> rejoiced on it, for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it. <hi type="super">6</hi> It shall be also carried unto Assyria <hi type="italic">for</hi> a present to king Jareb: Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water. <hi type="super">8</hi> The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us. <div eID="gen19878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19879" type="x-p"/> Observe, I. What the sins are which are here laid to Israel's charge, the national sins which bring down national judgment. The prophet deals plainly with them; for what good would it do them to be flattered? <div eID="gen19879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19880" type="x-p"/> 1. They were not fruitful in the fruits of righteousness to the glory of God. Here all their other wickedness began (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Israel is an empty vine.</hi> The church of God is fitly compared to a <hi type="italic">vine,</hi> weak, and of an unpromising outside, yet spreading and fruitful; believers are branches of that vine, and partake of its root and fatness. But this was the character of Israel, they were as <hi type="italic">an empty vine,</hi> a vine that had no sap or virtue in it, and therefore none of those good fruits produced by it that were expected from it, with which God and man should be honoured. Note, There are many who, though they have not become <hi type="italic">degenerate</hi> vines, are yet <hi type="italic">empty vines,</hi> have no good in them. A vine is of all trees least serviceable if it do not bear fruit. It is thenceforth good for nothing, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.3">Ezek. xv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.5">5</reference>. And those that bring forth no grapes will soon come to bring forth wild grapes; those that do no good will do hurt. He is an <hi type="italic">empty vine,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he brings forth fruit to himself.</hi> What good there is in him is not directed to the glory of God, but he takes the praise of it to himself, and prides himself in it. Christians live not to themselves (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Rom. xiv. 6</reference>), but hypocrites make self their centre; they <hi type="italic">eat and drink to themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5-Zech.7.6">Zech. vii. 5, 6</reference>. Or Israel is by the judgments of God <hi type="italic">emptied</hi> and <hi type="italic">spoiled</hi> of all his wealth, because he made use of it in the service of his lusts, and not to the honour of God who gave it to him. Note, What we do not rightly employ we may justly expect to be emptied of. <div eID="gen19880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19881" type="x-p"/> 2. They multiplied their altars and images, and the more bountiful God's providence was to them the more prodigal they were in serving their idols: <hi type="italic">According to the multitude of his fruit</hi> which his land brought forth <hi type="italic">he has increased the altars,</hi> and <hi type="italic">according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.</hi> Note, It is a great affront to God, and an abuse of his goodness, when the more mercies we receive from him the more sins we commit against him, and when the more wealth men have the more mischief they do. Should not we be thus abundant in the service of our God, as they were in the service of their idols? As we find our estates increasing, we should proportionably abound the more in works of piety and charity. <div eID="gen19881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19882" type="x-p"/> 3. Their hearts were divided, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.2">v. 2</reference>. (1.) They were divided among themselves. They were at variance about their idols, some for one, some for another, at variance about their kings, whose separate interests made parties in the kingdom, and in them their very hearts were divided, and alienated one from another, and there was no such thing as cordial friendship to be found among them; it follows therefore, <hi type="italic">Now shall they be found faulty.</hi> Note, The divisions and animosities of a people are the causes of much sin and the presages of ruin. (2.) They were divided between God and their idols. They had a remaining affection in their hearts for God, but a reigning affection for their idols. They <hi type="italic">halted between God and Baal,</hi> that was the dividing of their heart. But God is the sovereign of the heart and he will by no means endure a rival; he will either have all or none. Satan, like the pretended mother, says, <hi type="italic">Let it be neither mine nor thine, but divide it;</hi> but, if this be yielded to, God says, Nay, <hi type="italic">let him take it all.</hi> A heart thus divided will be <hi type="italic">found faulty,</hi> and be rejected as treacherous in covenanting with God. Note, A heart divided between God and mammon, though it may trim the matter so as to appear plausible, will, in the day of discovery, be <hi type="italic">found faulty.</hi> <div eID="gen19882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19883" type="x-p"/> 4. They made no conscience of what they said and what they did in the most solemn manner, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">v. 4</reference> (1.) Not of what they said in swearing, which is the most solemn speaking: <hi type="italic">They have spoken words,</hi> and words only, for they meant not as they said; they did <hi type="italic">verba dare—give words.</hi> They <hi type="italic">swore falsely in making a covenant;</hi> they were deceitful in their covenanting with God, the covenant of circumcision, the fair promises they made of reformation when they were in distress; and no marvel if those that were false to their God were false to all mankind. They contracted such a habit of treachery that they broke through the most sacred bonds, and made nothing of them; subjects violated their oaths of allegiance and their kings their coronation-oaths; they broke their leagues with the nations they were in alliance with, nor was any conscience made of contracts between private persons. (2.) Nor of what they did in judgment, which is the most solemn acting. Justice could not take place when men made nothing of forswearing themselves; for thus <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> which should have been a healing medicinal plant and of a sweet smell, <hi type="italic">sprang up as hemlock,</hi> which is both nauseous and noxious, <hi type="italic">in the furrows of the field,</hi> in the field that was ploughed and furrowed for good corn. Note, God is greatly offended with corruptions, not only in his own worship, but in the administration of justice between man and man, and the dishonesty of a people shall be the ground of his controversy with them as well as their idolatry and impiety; for God's laws are intended for man's benefit and the good of the community, as well as for God's honour, and the profanation of courts of justice shall be avenged as surely as the profanation of temples. <div eID="gen19883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19884" type="x-p"/> II. What the judgments are with which Israel should be punished for these sins; they sinned both in civil and religious matters, and in both they shall be punished. 1. They shall have no joy of their kings and of their government. Because justice is turned into oppression, therefore those who are entrusted with the administration of it, and should be blessings to the state, shall be complained of as the burdens of it (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.3">v. 3</reference>), and those that would not rule their people well shall not be able to protect them: <hi type="italic">Now they shall say, "We have no king,</hi> that is, we are as if we had none, we have none to do us any good nor stand us in any stead, none to keep us from destroying ourselves or being destroyed by our enemies, none to preserve the public peace nor to fight our battles; and justly has this come to us. <hi type="italic">Because we feared not the Lord,</hi> when we were safe under the protection of our kings, therefore we are rejected by him, and then <hi type="italic">what shall a king do for us?</hi> What good can we expect from a king when we have forfeited the favour of our God?" Note, Those that cast off the fear of God are not likely to have joy of any of their creature-comforts; nor will men's loyalty to their prince befriend them without religion, for, though that may engage him to be for them, what good will that do them if God be against them? Those that keep themselves in the fear and favour of God may say, with triumph, "What can the greatest of men do against us?" But those that throw themselves out of his protection must say, with despair, "What can the greatest of men do for us?" He was a king that said, <hi type="italic">If the Lord do not help thee, whence should I help thee?</hi> Yet he is a fool that says, If a king cannot help us, we must perish (as these intimate here), for God can do that for us which kings cannot. Time was when they doted upon having a king; but now what can a king (who, they thought, could do any thing) do for them? God can make people sick of those creature-confidences which they were most fond of. This is their complaint when their king is disabled to help them, yet this is not the worst; their civil government shall not only be weakened, but quite destroyed (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">As for Samaria,</hi> the royal city, which is now almost all that is left, <hi type="italic">her king is cut off as the foam from the water.</hi> The foam swims uppermost, and makes a great show upon the face of the water, yet it is but a heap of bubbles raised by the troubling of the water. Such were the kings of Israel, after their revolt from the house of David, a mere scum; their government had no foundation. No better are the greatest of kings when they set up in opposition to God; when God comes to contend with them by his judgments he can as easily disperse and dissolve them, and bring them to nothing, as the froth upon the water. 2. They shall have no joy of their idols and of their worship of them. And miserable is the case of that people whose gods fail them when their kings do. (1.) The idols they had made, and the altars they had set up in honour of them, should be broken down, and spoiled, and carried away, as common plunder, by the victorious enemy: He <hi type="italic">shall break down their altars.</hi> God shall do it by the hand of the Assyrians: the Assyrians shall do it by order from God. <hi type="italic">He shall spoil their images,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.10.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, What men make idols of it is just with God to <hi type="italic">break down</hi> and <hi type="italic">spoil.</hi> But the calf at Bethel was the sovereign idol; it was this that the inhabitants of Samaria doted most upon; now it is here foretold that this should be destroyed: <hi type="italic">The glory of it has departed from it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.5">v. 5</reference>) when it is thrown down and defaced, no more to be worshipped; but this is not all: <hi type="italic">It shall also be carried to Assyria</hi> (as some think that the calf at Dan was some time before) <hi type="italic">for a present to king Jareb.</hi> It was carried to him as a rich booty (for it was a golden calf, and probably adorned with the gifts and offerings of its worshippers) and as a trophy of victory over their enemies: and what more glorious trophy could they bring than this, or more incontestable proof of an absolute conquest? Thus it is said, <hi type="italic">The sin of Israel shall be destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">v. 8</reference>), that is, the idols which they made the matter of their sin; it is said of them, <hi type="italic">They became a sin to all Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.30">1 Kings xii. 30</reference>. Note, If the grace of God prevail not to destroy the love of sin in us, it is just that the providence of God should destroy the food and fuel of sin about us. With the idols, <hi type="italic">the high places</hi> shall be destroyed, the <hi type="italic">high places of Aven,</hi> that is, of <hi type="italic">Bethaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.5">v. 5</reference>) or <hi type="italic">Bethel;</hi> it was called <hi type="italic">the house of God</hi> (so Bethel signifies), but now it is called <hi type="italic">the house of iniquity,</hi> nay, <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> itself. The kings did not, as they ought to have done, <hi type="italic">take away the high places</hi> by the sword of justice, and therefore God will take them away by the sword of war; so that <hi type="italic">the thorn and the thistle</hi> shall <hi type="italic">come up on their altars,</hi> that is, they shall lie in ruins. Their altars, while they stood, were as thorns and thistles, offensive to God and good men, and fruits of sin and the curse; justly therefore are they buried in thorns and thistles. (2.) The destruction of their idols, their altars, and their high places, shall be the occasion of sorrow, and shame, and terror to them. [1.] It shall be an occasion of sorrow to them. When the calf at Bethel is broken <hi type="italic">the people thereof shall mourn over it.</hi> They looked upon the calf to be the protector of their nation, and, when that was gone, thought they must all be undone, which made the poor ignorant people that were deluded into the love of it lament bitterly, as Micah did (<reference osisRef="Judg.18.24">Judg. xviii. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">You have taken away my gods, and what have I more?</hi> The priests that had rejoiced in it shall now mourn for it with the people. Note, Whatever men make a god of they will mourn for the loss of; and an inordinate sorrow for the loss of any worldly good is a sign we made an idol of it. They used to be very merry in the worship of their idols, but now they shall mourn over them; for sinful mirth shall, sooner or later, be turned into mourning. [2.] It shall be an occasion of shame to them (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ephraim shall receive shame</hi> when he sees the gods he trusted to carried into captivity, and <hi type="italic">Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel,</hi> in putting such confidence in them and paying such adoration to them. God's ark and altars were never thrown down till the people rejected them; but the idolatrous altars were thrown down when the people were doting on them, which shows that the contempt of the former, and the veneration for the latter, were the sins for which God visited them. [3.] It shall be an occasion of fear to them (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear;</hi> they shall be in pain for their gods and afraid of losing them; or, rather, they shall be in pain for themselves and their children and families, when they see the judgments of God breaking in upon them and beginning with their idols, as he <hi type="italic">executed judgment against the gods of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exod. xii. 12</reference>. Thus idolaters are brought in trembling when God arises to <hi type="italic">shake terribly the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 21</reference>. And here (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">They shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.</hi> The supporters of idolatry (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15-Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 15, 16</reference>) are brought in calling thus in vain to rocks and mountains to shelter them from God's wrath.
entries.6fd87a2b710f09ed2f1bc100649979218b815441: <div eID="gen19884" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 730.)</title> <div sID="gen19885" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them. <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> in my desire that I should chastise them; and the people shall be gathered against them, when they shall bind themselves in their two furrows. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Ephraim <hi type="italic">is as</hi> a heifer <hi type="italic">that is</hi> taught, <hi type="italic">and</hi> loveth to tread out <hi type="italic">the corn;</hi> but I passed over upon her fair neck: I will make Ephraim to ride; Judah shall plow, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Jacob shall break his clods. <hi type="super">12</hi> Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> time to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , till he come and rain righteousness upon you. <hi type="super">13</hi> Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity; ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people, and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled, as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle: the mother was dashed in pieces upon <hi type="italic">her</hi> children. <hi type="super">15</hi> So shall Bethel do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off. <div eID="gen19885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19886" type="x-p"/> Here, I. They are put in mind of the sins of their fathers and predecessors, for which God would now reckon with them. It was told them (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">ch. ix. 9</reference>) that they had <hi type="italic">corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah,</hi> and here (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah.</hi> Not only the wickedness that was committed in that age is revived in this, and reacted, a copy from that original, but the wickedness that was committed in that age has been continued in a constant series and succession through all the intervening ages down to this; so that the measure of iniquity had been long in filling; and still there had been made additions to it. Or, "<hi type="italic">Thou has sinned more than in the days of Gibeah</hi>" (so it may be read); "the sins of this age exceed those of the worst of former ages. The case was bad then, for <hi type="italic">there they stood;</hi> the criminals stood in their own defence, and the tribes of Israel, who undertook to chastise them for their wickedness, were <hi type="italic">at a stand,</hi> when both in the first and in the second battle the malefactors were the victors; and <hi type="italic">the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them</hi> till the third engagement, and then did not overtake them all, for 600 made their escape. But thy sin is worse than theirs, and therefore thou canst not expect but that the battle against the children of iniquity should overtake thee, and overcome thee." <div eID="gen19886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19887" type="x-p"/> II. They have warning given them, fair warning, of the judgments of God that were coming upon them, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.10">v. 10</reference>. God had hitherto pitied and spared them. Though they had been very provoking, he had a mind to try whether they would be wrought upon by patience and forbearance; but now, "<hi type="italic">It is in my desire that I should chastise them;</hi> it is what I have a purpose of and will take pleasure in." He will <hi type="italic">rejoice over them to do them hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">Deut. xxviii. 63</reference>. Note, Because God does not desire the death and ruin of sinners, therefore he does desire their chastisement. And see what the chastisement it: <hi type="italic">The people shall be gathered against them,</hi> as all the other tribes were against Benjamin in the battle of Gibeah. One of the rabbin thus descants upon it: "Because they receive not chastisement from me by my prophets, who in my name rebuke them, I will chastise them by the hands of the people who shall be <hi type="italic">gathered against them, when they shall bind themselves in their two furrows,</hi>" that is, when they shall think to fortify themselves, as it were, within a double entrenchment. Or, <hi type="italic">When I shall bind them for their two transgressions</hi> (so the margin reads it), meaning their corporal and spiritual whoredom, which they are so often charged with, or the <hi type="italic">two calves</hi> at Dan and Bethel, or those two great evils mentioned <reference osisRef="Jer.2.12">Jer. ii. 13</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">When I shall bind them to their two furrows,</hi> that is, bring them into servitude to the Assyrians, who shall keep them under the yoke as oxen in the plough, who are bound to the two furrows up the field and down it, and dare not, for fear of the goad, stir a step out of them. The Chaldee says, Those that are <hi type="italic">gathered against them shall exercise dominion over them, in like manner as a pair of heifers are tied to their two furrows.</hi> Thus those that would not be God's freemen shall be their enemies' slaves, and shall be made to know the difference between <hi type="italic">God's service</hi> and <hi type="italic">the service of the kingdoms of the countries,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2 Chron. xii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen19887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19888" type="x-p"/> III. They are made to know that their unacquaintedness with sufferings and hardships should not excuse them from a very miserable captivity, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">v. 11</reference>. See how nice, and tender, and delicate, Ephraim is; he is <hi type="italic">as a heifer that is taught to tread out the corn, and loves</hi> that work, because, being not allowed to be muzzled, she has liberty to eat at pleasure, and the work itself was dry and easy, and both its own diversion and its own wages. "But," says God, "I have a yoke to put upon <hi type="italic">her fair neck,</hi> fair as it is. <hi type="italic">I will make Ephraim to ride,</hi> that is, I will tame them, or cause them to be ridden by the Assyrians and other conquerors that shall rule them with rigour, as men do the beasts they ride upon (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>); and <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> too shall be made to <hi type="italic">plough,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jacob to break the clods,</hi>" that is, they shall be used hardly, but not so hardly as Ephraim. Note, It is just with God to make those know what hardships mean that indulge themselves too much in their own ease and pleasure. The learned Dr. Pocock inclines to another sense of these words, as intimating the tender gentle methods God took with this people, to bring them into obedience to his law, as a reason why they should return to that obedience; he had managed them as the husbandman does his cattle that he trains up for service. Ephraim being as a docile heifer, fit to be employed, God took hold of <hi type="italic">her fair neck,</hi> to accustom her to the hand, <hi type="italic">harnessed her,</hi> or put the yoke of his commandments upon her, gave his people Israel a law, that, being trained up in his institutions, they might not be tempted by the usages of the heathen; he had used all fair and likely means with them to keep them in their obedience, had set <hi type="italic">Judah to plough</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jacob to break the clods,</hi> had employed them in the observance of precepts proper for them; and yet they would not be retained in their obedience, but started aside. <div eID="gen19888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19889" type="x-p"/> IV. They are invited and encouraged to return to God by prayer, repentance, and reformation, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12-Hos.10.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. See here, <div eID="gen19889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19890" type="x-p"/> 1. The duties they are called to. They are <hi type="italic">God's husbandry</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1 Cor. iii. 9</reference>), and the duties are expressed in language borrowed from the husbandman's calling. If they would not be brought into bondage by their oppressors, let them return to God's service. (1.) Let them <hi type="italic">break up the fallow ground;</hi> let them cleanse their hearts from all corrupt affections and lusts, which are as weeds and thorns, and let them be humbled for their sins, and be of a broken and contrite spirit in the sense of them; let them be full of sorrow and shame at the remembrance of them, and prepare to receive the divine precepts, as the ground that is ploughed is to receive the seed, that it may take root. See <reference osisRef="Jer.4.3">Jer. iv. 3</reference>. (2.) Let them <hi type="italic">sow to themselves in righteousness;</hi> let them return to the practice of good works, according to the law of God, which is the rule of righteousness; let them abound in works of piety towards God, and of justice and charity towards one another, and herein let them <hi type="italic">sow to the Spirit,</hi> as the apostle speaks, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 7, 8</reference>. Every action is seed sown. Let them <hi type="italic">sow in righteousness;</hi> let them sow what they should sow, do what they should do, and they themselves shall have the benefit of it. (3.) Let them <hi type="italic">seek the Lord;</hi> let them look up to him for his grace, and beg of him to bless the <hi type="italic">seed sown.</hi> The husbandman must plough and sow with an eye to God, asking of him rain in the season thereof. <div eID="gen19890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19891" type="x-p"/> 2. The arguments used for the pressing of these duties. Consider, (1.) It is time to do it; it is <hi type="italic">high time.</hi> The husbandman sows in seed-time, and, if that time be far spent, he applies to the work with the more diligence. Note, Seeking the Lord is to be every day's work, but there are some special occasions given by the providence and grace of God when it is, in a particular manner, time to seek him. (2.) If we do our part, God will do his. If we <hi type="italic">sow to ourselves in righteousness</hi>—if we be careful and diligent to do our duty, in a dependence upon his grace—he will shower down his grace upon us, will <hi type="italic">rain righteousness,</hi> the very thing that those need most who are to sow <hi type="italic">in righteousness;</hi> for <hi type="italic">by the grace of God we are what we are.</hi> Some apply it to Christ, who should come in the fulness of time, and for whose coming they must prepare themselves; he shall come as <hi type="italic">the Lord our righteousness,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">rain righteousness upon us,</hi> that everlasting righteousness which he has brought in; he will grant us of it abundantly. It is foretold (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Ps. lxxii. 6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">he shall come down like rain.</hi> (3.) If we <hi type="italic">sow in righteousness,</hi> we shall <hi type="italic">reap in mercy,</hi> which agrees with that promise, If we <hi type="italic">sow to the Spirit,</hi> we shall <hi type="italic">of the Spirit reap life everlasting.</hi> We shall reap <hi type="italic">according to the measure of mercy</hi> (so the word is); it shall be a great reward, according to the <hi type="italic">riches of mercy,</hi> such a reward, not as becomes such mean creatures as we are to receive, but as becomes a God of infinite mercy to give, a reward, <hi type="italic">not of debt,</hi> but <hi type="italic">of grace.</hi> We reap not in merit, but in mercy. It is what is sown; God gives a body as it has pleased him. (4.) We have <hi type="italic">ploughed wickedness and reaped iniquity;</hi> and the time <hi type="italic">past of our life may suffice</hi> that we have done so, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.13">v. 13</reference>. "You have taken a great deal of pains in the service of sin, have laboured at it in the very fire; and will you grudge to bear the burden and heat of the day in God's service and in doing that which will be for your own advantage? You have done much to damn your souls; will you not undo it again, and do something to save them?" (5.) We never got any thing in the service of sin. They have <hi type="italic">ploughed wickedness</hi> (that is, they have done the drudgery of sin), and they have <hi type="italic">reaped iniquity,</hi> that is, they have got all that is to be got by it; they have carried it on to the <hi type="italic">harvest,</hi> and what the better? It is all a cheat. <hi type="italic">They have eaten the fruit of lies,</hi> fruit that is but a lie, which looks fair, but is rotten within; the <hi type="italic">works of darkness</hi> are <hi type="italic">unfruitful works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Eph. v. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Rom. vi. 21</reference>. Even the gains of sin yield the sinner no satisfaction. (6.) As our comforts, so our confidences, in the service of sin will certainly fail us: "<hi type="italic">Thou didst trust in thy ways, in the multitude of thy mighty men;</hi> thou has stayed thyself upon creatures, thy own power and policy, and therefore hast ventured to plough wickedness, and thy hopes have deceived thee; come therefore, and seek the Lord, and thy hope in him shall not deceive thee." <div eID="gen19891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19892" type="x-p"/> V. They are threatened with utter destruction, both for their carnal practices and for their carnal confidences, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.14-Hos.10.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because thou has sown wickedness, and trusted in thy own way, <hi type="italic">a tumult shall arise among thy people,</hi> either by insurrections at home or invasions from abroad, either of which will put a kingdom into confusion and make a noise, much more both together. 1. Their cities and strongholds shall be a prey to the enemy: The <hi type="italic">fortresses</hi> which they confided in, and in which they had laid up their effects, shall be seized and rifled, as <hi type="italic">Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle.</hi> This refers to some event that had lately happened, not elsewhere recorded; and probably Shalman is the same with Shalmaneser king of Assyria, who had lately put some town, or castle, or house (<hi type="italic">Beth-arbel is the house of Arbel</hi>), under <hi type="italic">military execution,</hi> which perhaps he used with severity in the beginning of his conquests, to terrify other garrisons into a speedy surrender at the first summons. God tells them that thus Samaria should be <hi type="italic">spoiled.</hi> 2. The inhabitants shall be put to the <hi type="italic">sword,</hi> as it was at <hi type="italic">Beth-arbel;</hi> when it was taken <hi type="italic">the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children,</hi> that is, they were both dashed in pieces together by the fury of the soldiers. See what cruel work war makes. <hi type="italic">Jusque datum sceleri—Wickedness has free course.</hi> It is strange that any of the human race could be so inhuman; but see what comes of sin. <hi type="italic">Homo homini lupus—Man is a wolf to man,</hi> and then, <hi type="italic">Homo homini agnus—Man is a lamb to man.</hi> 3. Even royal blood shall be mingled with common gore: <hi type="italic">In a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">v. 15</reference>. Hoshea was the last king of Israel; in him the whole kingdom was <hi type="italic">cut off</hi> and came to a period; it may refer either to him or to some of his predecessors that were cut off by treachery. It shall be done <hi type="italic">in a morning,</hi> in a very little time, as suddenly as the dawning of the morning, or at the time appointed, for so the morning comes, punctually at its time. Or <hi type="italic">in the morning,</hi> when they think the night of calamity is over, and expect a returning day, then shall all their hopes be dashed by the sudden cutting off of their king, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.7">v. 7</reference>. Kings, though gods to us, are men to God, and shall die like men. And (<hi type="italic">lastly</hi>) what does all this desolation owe its rise to? What is the spring of this bloodshed? He tells us (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">So shall Bethel do unto you.</hi> Bethel was the place where one of the calves was; Gilgal, where <hi type="italic">all their wickedness</hi> is said to have been, was hard by; there was their <hi type="italic">great wickedness,</hi> the <hi type="italic">evil of their evil</hi> (so the word is), the sum and quintessence of their sin; and that was it that <hi type="italic">did this to them,</hi> that made all this havoc, for that was it that provoked God to bring it upon them. He does not say, "So shall the <hi type="italic">king of Assyria</hi> do to you;" but, "So shall <hi type="italic">Bethel</hi> do to you." Note, Whatever mischief is done to us it is sin that does it. Are the fortresses spoiled? Are the women and children murdered? Is the king cut off? It is sin that does all this. It is sin that ruins soul, body, estate, all. <hi type="italic">So shall Bethel do unto you.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">thy own wickedness</hi> that <hi type="italic">corrects thee</hi> and <hi type="italic">thy backslidings</hi> that <hi type="italic">reprove thee.</hi>  <chapter eID="Hos.10"/> <div eID="gen19892" type="x-p"/>

entries.8ba1b1faa97db8bd0e2889014e0dfcea90995b01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12369"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.10.1-Hos.10.15">Ho 10:1-15</reference>. Israel's Idolatry, the Source of Perjuries and Unlawful Leagues, Soon Destined to Be the Ruin of the State, Their King and Their Images Being About to Be Carried Off; a Just Chastisement, the Reaping Corresponding to the Sowing.</title> <div sID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> The prophecy was uttered between Shalmaneser's first and second invasions of Israel. Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.10.14">Ho 10:14</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">Ho 10:6</reference>, referring to Hoshea's calling So of Egypt to his aid; also <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">Ho 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.13">13</reference>.<div eID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12369"/><hi type="bold">1. empty--</hi>stripped of its fruits [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Na 2:2</reference>); compelled to pay tribute to Pul (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.20">2Ki 15:20</reference>). Maurer translates, "A widespreading vine"; so the Septuagint. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Ge 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9-Ps.80.11">Psa 80:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.6">Eze 17:6</reference>.<div eID="gen22629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bringeth forth fruit unto himself--</hi>not unto Me.<div eID="gen22630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to ... multitude of ... fruit ... increased ... altars--</hi>In proportion to the abundance of their prosperity, which called for fruit unto God (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.6.22">Ro 6:22</reference>), was the abundance of their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Ho 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen22631" type="x-p"/>
entries.c64a7477823c38537e1a97d4db661ce413506ddc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12370"/><div sID="gen22632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12370"/><hi type="bold">2. heart ... divided--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">1Ki 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jas 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>that is, soon.<div eID="gen22633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen22634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break down--</hi>"cut off," namely the heads of the victims. Those altars, which were the scene of cutting off the victims' heads, shall be themselves cut off. <div eID="gen22635" type="x-p"/>
entries.0779febdb1e1879f4f19771484a88cf5448ce8ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12371"/><div sID="gen22636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12371"/><hi type="bold">3. now, &c.--</hi>Soon they, deprived of their king, shall be reduced to say, We have no king (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.7">Ho 10:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">15</reference>), for Jehovah deprived us of him, because of our not fearing God. What then (seeing God is against us) should a king be able to do for us, if we had one? As they rejected the heavenly King, they were deprived of their earthly king. <div eID="gen22636" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ff83098c4bbaf720bfcca249a61b9b3efa34e93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12372"/><div sID="gen22637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12372"/><hi type="bold">4. words--</hi>mere empty words.<div eID="gen22637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swearing falsely in making a covenant--</hi>breaking their engagement to Shalmaneser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>), and making a covenant with So, though covenants with foreigners were forbidden.<div eID="gen22638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment ... as hemlock--</hi>that is, divine judgment shall spring up as rank, and as deadly, as hemlock in the furrows (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.18">De 29:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Am 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.12">6:12</reference>). Gesenius translates, "poppy." Grotius, "darnel." <div eID="gen22639" type="x-p"/>
entries.6aa18e3d177b14acd53427ea2d950ee03030d233: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12373"/><div sID="gen22640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12373"/><hi type="bold">5. fear because of the calves--</hi>that is, shall fear for them.<div eID="gen22640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-aven--</hi>substituted for Beth-el in contempt (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it--</hi>singular, the one in Beth-el; after the pattern of which the other "calves" (plural) were made. "Calves" in the Hebrew is feminine, to express contempt.<div eID="gen22642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priests--</hi>The Hebrew is only used of idolatrous priests (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.4">Zep 1:4</reference>), from a root meaning either "the black garment" in which they were attired; or, "to resound," referring to their howling cries in their sacred rites [Calvin].<div eID="gen22643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that rejoiced on it--</hi>because it was a source of gain to them. Maurer translates, "Shall leap in trepidation on account of it"; as Baal's priests did (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1Ki 18:26</reference>).<div eID="gen22644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the glory thereof--</hi>the magnificence of its ornaments and its worship. <div eID="gen22645" type="x-p"/>
entries.b544f57291ba1f3ad1ef80c52f940d02e7988f61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12374"/><div sID="gen22646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12374"/><hi type="bold">6. It ... also--</hi>The calf, so far from saving its worshippers from deportation, itself shall be carried off; hence "Israel shall be ashamed" of it.<div eID="gen22646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jareb--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>). "A present to the king (whom they looked to as) their defender," or else avenger, whose wrath they wished to appease, namely, Shalmaneser. The minor states applied this title to the Great King, as the avenging Protector.<div eID="gen22647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own counsel--</hi>the calves, which Jeroboam set up as a stroke of policy to detach Israel from Judah. Their severance from Judah and Jehovah proved now to be not politic, but fatal to them. <div eID="gen22648" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b15b34f596c588840d613b6991984e4a8f04e1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12375"/><div sID="gen22649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12375"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.3">Ho 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen22649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foam--</hi>denoting short-lived existence and speedy dissolution. As the foam, though seeming to be eminent raised on the top of the water, yet has no solidity, such is the throne of Samaria. Maurer translates, "a chip" or broken branch that cannot resist the current. <div eID="gen22650" type="x-p"/>
entries.2be166270c18416197fc94fdebf0e56b32862b46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12376"/><div sID="gen22651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12376"/><hi type="bold">8. Aven--</hi>that is, Beth-aven.<div eID="gen22651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sin--</hi>that is, the occasion of sin (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">De 9:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.30">1Ki 12:30</reference>).<div eID="gen22652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall say to ... mountains, Cover us--</hi>So terrible shall be the calamity, that men shall prefer death to life (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.30">Lu 23:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Re 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.6">9:6</reference>). Those very hills on which were their idolatrous altars (one source of their confidence, as their "king," <reference osisRef="Hos.10.7">Ho 10:7</reference>, was the other), so far from helping them, shall be called on by them to overwhelm them. <div eID="gen22653" type="x-p"/>
entries.652e30fbe84d3362225de42cab2c64ff93975b91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12377"/><div sID="gen22654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12377"/><hi type="bold">9. Gibeah--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Ho 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.19.1-Judg.20.48">Jud 19:1-20:48</reference>). They are singled out as a specimen of the whole nation.<div eID="gen22654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there they stood--</hi>The Israelites have, as there and then, so ever since, persisted in their sin [Calvin]. Or, better, "they stood their ground," that is, did not perish then [Maurer].<div eID="gen22655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the battle ... did not overtake them--</hi>Though God spared you then, He will not do so now; nay, the battle whereby God punished the Gibeonite "children of iniquity," shall the more heavily visit you for your continued impenitence. Though "they stood" then, it shall not be so now. The change from "thou" to "they" marks God's alienation from them; they are, by the use of the third person, put to a greater distance from God. <div eID="gen22656" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c8c589f9b48d0f80f30517b5c3d02d9c18bc3aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12378"/><div sID="gen22657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12378"/><hi type="bold">10. my desire ... chastise--</hi>expressing God's strong inclination to vindicate His justice against sin, as being the infinitely holy God (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">De 28:63</reference>).<div eID="gen22657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people--</hi>Foreign invaders "shall be gathered against them."<div eID="gen22658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when they shall bind themselves in their two furrows--</hi>image from two oxen ploughing together side by side, in two contiguous furrows: so the Israelites shall join themselves, to unite their powers against all dangers, but it will not save them from My destroying them [Calvin]. Their "two furrows" may refer to their two places of setting up the calves, their ground of confidence, Dan and Beth-el; or, the two divisions of the nation, Israel and Judah, "in their two furrows," that is, in their respective two places of habitation; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference>, which specifies the two, favors this view. Henderson prefers the Keri (Hebrew Margin) "for their two iniquities"; and translates, "when they are bound" in captivity. English Version is best, as the image is carried out in <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference>; only it is perhaps better to translate, "the people (the invaders) binding them," that is, making them captives; and so <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference> alludes to the yoke being put on the neck of Ephraim and Judah. <div eID="gen22659" type="x-p"/>
entries.5930e3823a4a35760dbf7aa96ae8b6b132a44455: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12379"/><div sID="gen22660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12379"/><hi type="bold">11. taught--</hi>that is, accustomed.<div eID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loveth to tread out ... corn--</hi>a far easier and more self-indulgent work than ploughing. In treading corn, cattle were not bound together under a yoke, but either trod it singly with their feet, or drew a threshing sledge over it (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Is 28:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">28</reference>): they were free to eat some of the corn from time to time, as the law required they should be unmuzzled (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>), so that they grew fat in this work. An image of Israel's freedom, prosperity, and self-indulgence heretofore. But now God will put the Assyrian yoke upon her, instead of freedom, putting her to servile work.<div eID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I passed over upon--</hi>I put the yoke upon.<div eID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make ... to ride--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.22">Job 30:22</reference>; that is, hurry Ephraim away to a distant region [Calvin]. Lyra translates, "I will make (the Assyrian) to ride upon Ephraim." Maurer, "I will make Ephraim to carry," namely, a charioteer.<div eID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his clods--</hi>"the clods before him." <div eID="gen22664" type="x-p"/>
entries.df303e6af3b0ec4bb87d5fc8e8580385aca6c84e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12380"/><div sID="gen22665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12380"/>12. Continuation of the image in <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.18">Pr 11:18</reference>). Act righteously and ye shall reap the reward; a reward not of debt, but of grace.<div eID="gen22665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in mercy--</hi>according to the measure of the divine "mercy," which over and above repays the goodness or "mercy" which we show to our fellow man (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.38">Lu 6:38</reference>).<div eID="gen22666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break ... fallow ground--</hi>Remove your superstitions and vices, and be renewed.<div eID="gen22667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek ... Lord, fill he come--</hi>Though not answered immediately, persevere unceasingly "till He come."<div eID="gen22668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rain--</hi>send down as a copious shower.<div eID="gen22669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>the reward of righteousness, that is, salvation, temporal and spiritual (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.23">1Sa 26:23</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference> ). <div eID="gen22670" type="x-p"/>
entries.ded41c76da7ef046217ffe3fe3ee57c0c26fabc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12381"/><div sID="gen22671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12381"/><hi type="bold">13. reaped iniquity--</hi>that is, the fruit of iniquity; as "righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">Ho 10:12</reference>) is "the fruit of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pr 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen22671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lies--</hi>false and spurious worship.<div eID="gen22672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trust in thy way--</hi>thy perverse way (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">Is 57:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.23">Jr 2:23</reference>), thy worship of false gods. This was their internal safeguard, as their external was "the multitude of their mighty men." <div eID="gen22673" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad1f8b272ec0dd05fc5356193b38f3035af95551: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12382"/><div sID="gen22674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12382"/><hi type="bold">14. tumult--</hi>a tumultuous war.<div eID="gen22674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among thy people--</hi>literally, "peoples": the war shall extend to the whole people of Israel, through all the tribes, and the peoples allied to her.<div eID="gen22675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel--</hi>that is, Shalmaneser, a compound name, in which the part common to it and the names of three other Assyrian kings, is omitted; Tiglath-pileser, Esar-haddon, Shar-ezer. So Jeconiah is abbreviated to Coniah. Arbel was situated in Naphtali in Galilee, on the border nearest Assyria. Against it Shalmaneser, at his first invasion of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">2Ki 17:3</reference>), vented his chief rage. God threatens Israel's fortresses with the same fate as Arbel suffered "in the day (on the occasion) of the battle" then well-known, though not mentioned elsewhere (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.34">2Ki 18:34</reference>). This event, close on the reign of Hezekiah, shows the inscription of Hosea (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.1">Ho 1:1</reference>) to be correct. <div eID="gen22676" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1e69c9db797a9f28c657e2fadea47f0d9ae4bab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12383"/><div sID="gen22677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12383"/><hi type="bold">15. So shall Beth-el do unto you--</hi>that is, Your idolatrous calf at Beth-el shall be the cause of a like calamity befalling you.<div eID="gen22677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your great wickedness--</hi>literally, "the wickedness of your wickedness."<div eID="gen22678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a morning--</hi>that is, speedily, as quickly as the dawn is put to flight by the rising sun (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Ho 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.3">13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Psa 30:5</reference>).<div eID="gen22679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king--</hi>Hoshea. <chapter eID="Hos.10"/>

entries.d431586785cc136be10f7844b94cc14313e7668b: <div eID="gen33811" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33812" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33813" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33813" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33812" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33814" type="x-p"/> This chapter treats of the same subject, but elegantly varied. It begins with comparing Israel to a fruitful vine but corrupted by too much prosperity, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Hos 10:1</reference>. It next reproves and threatens them for their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.2">Hos 10:2</reference>; anarchy, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.3">Hos 10:3</reference>; and breach of covenant, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">Hos 10:4</reference>. Their idolatry is then enlarged on; and its fatal consequences declared in terms full of sublimity and pathos, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.5-Hos.10.8">Hos 10:5-8</reference>. God is now introduced complaining of their excessive guilt; and threatening them with captivity in terms that bear a manifest allusion to their favourite idolatry, the worshiping the similitude of a calf or heifer, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.9-Hos.10.11">Hos 10:9-11</reference>. Upon which the prophet, in a beautiful allegory suggested by the preceding metaphors, exhorts them to repentance; and warns them of the dreadful consequences of their evil courses, if obstinately persisted in, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12-Hos.10.15">Hos 10:12-15</reference>. <div eID="gen33814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33815" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33816" type="x-p"/> Israel is an empty vine - Or, a vine that casteth its grapes. <div eID="gen33816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33817" type="x-p"/> He bringeth forth fruit - Or, he laid up fruit for himself. He abused the blessings of God to the purposes of idolatry. He was prosperous; but his prosperity corrupted his heart. <div eID="gen33817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33818" type="x-p"/> According to the multitude of his fruit - He became idolatrous in proportion to his prosperity; and in proportion to their wealth was the costliness of their images, and the expensiveness of their idol worship. <div eID="gen33818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33819" type="x-p"/> True is the homely saying of old Quarles: - "So God's best gifts, usurp'd by wicked ones, <div eID="gen33819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33820" type="x-p"/> To poison turn, by their con-ta-gi-ons." <div eID="gen33820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33821" type="x-p"/> Another poet, of a higher order, but worse school, says: - <div eID="gen33821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33822" type="x-p"/> Effodiuntur opes, irritamenta malorum. <div eID="gen33822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33823" type="x-p"/> Ovid. <div eID="gen33823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33824" type="x-p"/> Of which the words of St. Paul are nearly a literal rendering: - Ῥιζα γαρ πανθων των κακων εστιν ἡ θιλαργυρια. "For the love of money is the root of all these evils" <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Tim 6:10</reference>. <div eID="gen33824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33825" type="x-p"/> Pity that this beautiful metal, on which God has bestowed such a large portion of mineral perfection, and then hid in the earth, should, on its being digged up by man, become the incentive to so many vices, and draw away his heart from the Creator of all things, and the fountain of ineffable perfection and goodness.
entries.b228e406a92abd1902668e8e7b241550bfe7c536: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33826" type="x-p"/> Their heart is divided - They wish to serve God and Mammon, Jehovah and Baal: but this is impossible. Now God will do in judgment what they should have done in contrition, "break down their altars, and spoil their images."
entries.3bdad90b21bd9e0aed1be78658332de31b7a531f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33827" type="x-p"/> We have no king - We have rejected the King of kings; and had we any king, he would be of no service to us in this state, as he would be a captive like ourselves; nor could we have the approbation of God, as we now justly lie under his displeasure.
entries.55feeb356686948ca3d56d99b96fc498d654153a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33828" type="x-p"/> They have spoken words - Vain, empty, deceitful words. <div eID="gen33828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33829" type="x-p"/> Swearing falsely - This refers to the alliances made with strange powers, to whom they promised fidelity without intending to be faithful; and from whom they promised themselves protection and support, notwithstanding God was against them, and they knew it. All their words were vain, and in the end as bitter as gall. <div eID="gen33829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33830" type="x-p"/> Judgment springeth up as hemlock - As our land lies without cultivation, so that we have nothing but noxious weeds instead of crops; so we have no administration of justice. What is done in this way is a perversion of law, and is as hurtful to society as hemlock would be to animal life. All this may refer to the anarchy that was in the kingdom of Israel before Hoshea's reign, and which lasted, according to Archbishop Usher, nine years. They then, literally, "had no king."
entries.933e210f0a55ecca6be02223338c2013ff149a39: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33831" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear - According to Calmet, shall worship the calves of Beth-aven; those set up by Jeroboam, at Beth-el. Fear is often taken for religious reverence. <div eID="gen33831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33832" type="x-p"/> The people thereof shall mourn - On seeing the object of their worship carried into captivity, as well as themselves. <div eID="gen33832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33833" type="x-p"/> And the priests thereof - כמרים kemarim. The priests of Samaria, says Calmet, are here called kemarim, that is, black coats, or shouters, because they made loud cries in their sacrifices. Instead of יגילו yagilu, "they shall rejoice;" learned men propose ילילו yalilu, "shall howl," which is likely to be the true reading, but it is not supported by any of the MSS. yet discovered. But the exigentia loci, the necessity of the place, requires some such word.
entries.c4b7928e5ba9c4900715eb3f4978c2b873a1baf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33834" type="x-p"/> A present to King Jareb - See on <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Hos 5:13</reference> (note). If this be a proper name, the person intended is not known in history: but it is most likely that Pul, king of Assyria, is intended, to whom Menahem, king of Israel, appears to have given one of the golden calves, to insure his assistance.
entries.4f2b46c28e933bc3a9d9f58728c9fa2ddae8b5e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33835" type="x-p"/> Her king is cut off as the foam - As lightly as a puff of wind blows off the foam that is formed below by a fall of water, so shall the kings of Israel be cut off. We have already seen that not less than four of them died by assassination in a very short time. See on <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">Hos 7:7</reference> (note).
entries.646ed7fad0e0480b3e3bb16626ba43c52261fa29: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33836" type="x-p"/> The high-places - Idol temples. <div eID="gen33836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33837" type="x-p"/> Of Aven - Beth-aven. <div eID="gen33837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33838" type="x-p"/> The thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars - Owing to the uncultivated and unfrequented state of the land, and of their places of idol worship, the people being all carried away into captivity. "And they shall say to the mountains, Cover us, And to the hills, Fall on us." "This sublime description of fear and distress our Lord had in view, <reference osisRef="Luk.23.30">Luk 23:30</reference>, which may be a reference, and not a quotation. However, the Septuagint, in the Codex Alexandrinus, has the same order of words as occurs in the evangelist. The parallelism makes the passages more beautiful than <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev 6:16</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference> wants the animated dramatic form. That there is a reference to the caverns that abounded in the mountainous countries of Palestine, see the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference> (note)." - Newcome.
entries.ce365ec13280dd9215d83af6455d43812893afce: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33839" type="x-p"/> Thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah - This is another reference to the horrible rape and murder of the Levite's wife, <reference osisRef="Jdg.19.13">Jdg 19:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.19.14">Jdg 19:14</reference>. <div eID="gen33839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33840" type="x-p"/> There they stood - Only one tribe was nearly destroyed, viz., that of Benjamin. They were the criminals, the children of iniquity; the others were faultless, and stood only for the rights of justice and mercy.
entries.7aa77f957ccf2e54b51d616b9340a86a9b587828: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33841" type="x-p"/> When they shall bind themselves in their two furrows - "When they are chastised for their two iniquities," i.e., the calves in Dan and Beth-el. - Newcome. But this double iniquity may refer to what Jeremiah says, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jer 11:13</reference> : "My people have committed two evils." - <div eID="gen33841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> 1. They have forsaken me. <div eID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> 2. They have joined themselves to idols.
entries.30f3d2c0281f3bd8f61adda96dc209affacd4d30: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33844" type="x-p"/> Ephraim is as a heifer that is taught - One thoroughly broken in to the yoke. <div eID="gen33844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33845" type="x-p"/> And loveth to tread out - Goes peaceably in the yoke; and is pleased because, not being muzzled, she eats of the corn. <div eID="gen33845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33846" type="x-p"/> I passed over upon her fair neck - I brought the yoke upon it, that she should not tread out the corn merely, but draw the plough and drag the harrow. These operations of husbandry are all referred to here, with some others. Ephraim shall tread out the corn, that there may be seed for the fields. <div eID="gen33846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33847" type="x-p"/> Judah shall plough - That the furrows may receive it. <div eID="gen33847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33848" type="x-p"/> Jacob shall break his clods - Harrow - that the seed may be covered with the mould. <div eID="gen33848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33849" type="x-p"/> Israel very frequently made great depredations on Judah; and as this heifer loved to tread out the corn, and not plough, it is therefore added that he should be made to plough, be put under the yoke, namely, that of the Assyrians. What is added, "Judah and Jacob shall plough for themselves," means, that Judah should not now plough for Israel, but for himself; as Israel shall no more make depredations upon him. - Dodd.
entries.2d11fd667395bc17716c5290de2262c5ecc4cc3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33850" type="x-p"/> Sow to yourselves in righteousness - Let the seed you sow be of the best kind, and in just measure. <div eID="gen33850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33851" type="x-p"/> Reap in mercy - By the blessing of God on this ploughing, sowing, and harrowing, you may expect a good crop in harvest. <div eID="gen33851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33852" type="x-p"/> Break up your fallow ground - Do not be satisfied with a slight furrow; let the land that was fallowed (slightly ploughed) be broken up again with a deep furrow. <div eID="gen33852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33853" type="x-p"/> For it is time to seek the Lord - This should be immediately done: the season is passing; and if you do not get the seed in the ground, the early rain will be past, and your fields will be unfruitful. <div eID="gen33853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33854" type="x-p"/> Rain righteousness upon you - God will give you the early rain in due time, and in proper measure. Here are the metaphors, and the application cannot be difficult.. Here are ploughing, fallowing, sowing, harrowing, watering, reaping, threshing, and feeding on the produce of well-directed labor. All may be applied to the human heart, and the work of God upon it. Correction, contrition, conversion, receiving the grace of Christ, bringing forth fruit, etc.
entries.eccd2ecc7de3e2206291d7cb327acfaf6a174149: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33855" type="x-p"/> Ye have ploughed wickedness - Ye have labored sinfully. <div eID="gen33855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33856" type="x-p"/> Ye have reaped iniquity - The punishment due to your iniquity. <div eID="gen33856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33857" type="x-p"/> Ye have eaten the fruit of lies - Your false worship and your false gods have brought you into captivity and misery. <div eID="gen33857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33858" type="x-p"/> Because thou didst trust in thy way - Didst confide in thy own counsels, and in thy mighty men, and not in the God who made you.
entries.a1aa7a7e854d96782ae99da8ee38b3afc711f0a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33859" type="x-p"/> Shall a tumult arise - The enemy shall soon fall upon thy people, and take all thy fortified places. <div eID="gen33859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33860" type="x-p"/> As Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel - Some think that this refers to Jerubbaal, or Gideon's victory over Zalmunna, general of the Midianites; see <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.8">Jdg 7:8</reference>. Others think that an allusion is made here to the destruction of Arbela, a city of Armenia, by Shalmaneser, here called Shalman; and this while he was only general of the Assyrian forces, and not yet king. I think the history to which this refers is unknown. It seems that it was distinguished by some remarkable ferocities. <div eID="gen33860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33861" type="x-p"/> The mother was dashed in pieces upon her children - But when, where, how, and by whom, still remain unknown. Conjecture in such a case must be useless.
entries.86a8e7f4fa58d86f53d46ea064fcf940b0b492f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33862" type="x-p"/> So shall Beth-el do unto you - This shall be the consequence of your idolatry. <div eID="gen33862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33863" type="x-p"/> In a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off - Suddenly, unexpectedly. Hoshea, the king of Israel, shall be cut off by the Assyrians. There are some allusions to facts in this chapter, which cannot be easily verified, as we have not sufficient acquaintance with the history of those times.  <chapter eID="Hos.10"/> <div eID="gen33863" type="x-p"/>

entries.4bcfb9422ab077dd52ea9e4fa28fc9fd5a5d27ac: Hos 10:1-3 <div eID="gen16247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16248" type="x-p"/> In a fresh turn the concluding thought of the last strophe (Hos 9:10) is resumed, and the guilt and punishment of Israel still more fully described in two sections, Hos 10:1-8 and Hos 10:9-15. Hos 10:1. <hi type="italic">“Israel is a running vine; it set fruit for itself: the more of its fruit, the more altars did it prepare; the better its land, the better pillars did they make.</hi> Hos 10:2. <hi type="italic">Smooth was their heart, ow will they atone. He will break in pieces their altars, desolate their pillars. </hi> Hos 10:3. <hi type="italic">Yea, now will they say, No king to us! for we feared not Jehovah; and the king, what shall he do to us?” </hi> Under the figure of a vine running luxuriantly, which did indeed set some good fruit, but bore no sound ripe grapes, the prophet describes Israel as a glorious plantation of God Himself, which did not answer the expectations of its Creator. The figure is simply sketched in a few bold lines. We have an explanatory parallel in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">Psa 80:9</reference>-12. The participle <hi type="italic">bōqēq</hi> does not mean “empty” or “emptying out” here; for this does not suit the next clause, according to which the fruit was set, but from the primary meaning of <hi type="italic">bâqaq</hi>, to pour out, pouring itself out, overflowing, i.e., running luxuriantly. It has the same meaning, therefore, as ג סרחת in <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.6">Eze 17:6</reference>, that which extends its branches far and wide, that is to say, grows most vigorously. The next sentence, “it set fruit,” still belongs to the figure; but in the third sentence the figure passes over into a literal prophecy. According to the abundance of its fruit, Israel made many altars; and in proportion to the goodness of its land, it made better מצּבות, Baal’s pillars (see at 1Ki 14:23); i.e., as Israel multiplied, and under the blessing of God attained to prosperity, wealth, and power in the good land (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>), it forgot its God, and fell more and more into idolatry (cf. Hos 2:10; Hos 8:4, Hos 8:11). The reason of all this was, that their heart was smooth, i.e., dissimulating, not sincerely devoted to the Lord, inasmuch as, under the appearance of devotedness to God, they still clung to idols (for the fact, see 2Ki 17:9). The word <hi type="italic">châlâq</hi>, to be smooth, was mostly applied by a Hebrew to the tongue, lip, mouth, throat, and speech (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Psa 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">Psa 55:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">Pro 5:3</reference>), and not to the heart. But in <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.24">Eze 12:24</reference> we read of <hi type="italic">smooth</hi>, i.e., deceitful prophesying; and there is all the more reason for retaining the meaning “smooth” here, that the rendering “their heart is divided,” which is supported by the ancient versions, cannot be grammatically defended. For <hi type="italic">châlâq</hi> is not used in <hi type="italic">kal</hi> in an intransitive sense; and the active rendering, “He (i.e., God) has divided their heart” (Hitzig), gives an unscriptural thought. They will now atone for this, for God will destroy their altars and pillars. ערף, “to break the neck of the altars,” is a bold expression, applied to the destruction of the altars by breaking off the horns (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.3.14">Amo 3:14</reference>). Then will the people see and be compelled to confess that it has no longer a king, because it has not feared the Lord, since the king who has been set up in opposition to the will of the Lord (Hos 8:4) cannot bring either help or deliverance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>). עשׂה, to do, i.e., to help or be of use to a person (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.2">Ecc 2:2</reference>).
entries.feaeed43a9cec594160d71be323990f892249ada: Hos 10:4-6 <div eID="gen16248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16249" type="x-p"/> The thoughts of Hos 10:2, Hos 10:3 are carried out still further in Hos 10:4-7. Hos 10:4. “They have spoken words, sworn falsely, made treaties: thus right springs up like darnel in the furrows of the field. Hos 10:5. For the calves of Beth-aven the inhabitants of Samaria were afraid: yea, its people mourn over it, and its sacred ministers will tremble at it, at its glory, because it has strayed from them. Hos 10:6. Men will also carry it to Asshur, as a present for king Jareb: shame will seize upon Ephraim, and Israel will be put to shame for its counsel.” The dissimulation of heart (Hos 10:3) manifested itself in their speaking words which were nothing but words, i.e., in vain talk (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Isa 58:13</reference>), in false swearing, and in the making of treaties. אלות, by virtue of the parallelism, is an infin. abs. for אלה, formed like כּרת, analogous to שׁתות (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Isa 22:13</reference>; see Ewald, §240, b). כּרת בּרית, in connection with false swearing, must signify the making of a covenant without any truthfulness in it, i.e., the conclusion of treaties with foreign nations - for example, with Assyria - which they were inclined to observe only so long as they could promise themselves advantages from them. In consequence of this, right has become like a bitter plant growing luxuriantly (ראשׁ = רושׁ; see at <reference osisRef="Deut.29.17">Deu 29:17</reference>). Mishpât does not mean judgment here, or the punitive judgment of God (Chald. and many others), for this could hardly be compared with propriety to weeds running over everything, but right in its degeneracy into wrong, or right that men have turned into bitter fruit or poison (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.12">Amo 6:12</reference>). This spreads about in the kingdom, as weeds spread luxuriantly in the furrows of the field (שׂדי a poetical form for שׂדה, like <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deu 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.8">Psa 8:8</reference>). Therefore the judgment cannot be delayed, and is already approaching in so threatening a manner, that the inhabitants of Samaria tremble for the golden calves. The plural ‛eglōth is used with indefinite generality, and gives no warrant, therefore, for the inference that there were several golden calves set up in Bethel. Moreover, this would be at variance with the fact, that in the sentences which follow we find “the (one) calf” spoken of. The feminine form ‛eglōth, which only occurs here, is also probably connected with the abstract use of the plural, inasmuch as the feminine is the proper form for abstracts. Bēth-'âven for Bēth-'ēl, as in Hos 4:15. Shâkhēn is construed with the plural, as an adjective used in a collective sense. כּי (Hos 4:5) is emphatic, and the suffixes attached to עמּו and כּמריו do not refer to Samaria, but to the idol, i.e., the calf, since the prophet distinctly calls Israel, which ought to have been the nation of Jehovah, the nation of its calf-idol, which mourned with its priests (kemârı̄m, the priests appointed in connection with the worship of the calves: see at 2Ki 23:5) for the carrying away of the calf to Assyria. גּיל does not mean to exult or rejoice here, nor to tremble (applied to the leaping of the heart from fear, as it does from joy), but has the same meaning as חיל in Psa 96:9. עליו is still further defined by על־כּבודו, “for its glory,” i.e., not for the temple-treasure at Bethel (Hitzig), nor the one glorious image of the calf, as the symbol of the state-god (Ewald, Umbreit), but the calf, to which the people attributed the glory of the true God. The perfect, gâlâh, is used prophetically of that which was as good as complete and certain (for the fut. exact., cf. Ewald, §343, a). The golden calf, the glory of the nation, will have to wander into exile. This cannot even save itself; it will be taken to Assyria, to king Jareb (see at Hos 5:13), as minchâh, a present of tribute (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>; 1Ki 5:1). For the construing of the passive with את, see Ges. §143, 1, a. Then will Ephraim (= Israel) be seized by reproach and shame. Boshnâh, a word only met with here; it is formed from the masculine bōshen, which is not used at all (see Ewald, §163, 164).
entries.e3c134ced4809c4b4c579c65cdb3b4a146e21ebf: Hos 10:7-8 <div eID="gen16249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16250" type="x-p"/> With the carrying away of the golden calf the kingdom of Samaria also perishes, and desert plants will grow upon the places of idols. Hos 10:7, Hos 10:8. <hi type="italic">“Destroyed is Samaria; her king like a splinter on the surface of the water. And destroyed are the high places of Aven, the sin of Israel: thorn and thistle will rise up on their altars; and they will speak to the mountains, Cover us! and to the hills, Fall on us!” </hi>שׁמרון מלכּהּ is not an asyndeton, “Samaria and its king;” but <hi type="italic">Shōmerōn</hi> is to be taken absolutely, “as for Samaria,” although, as a matter of fact, not only Samaria, the capital of the kingdom, but the kingdom itself, was destroyed. For <hi type="italic">malkâh</hi> does not refer to any particular king, but is used in a general sense for “the king that Samaria had,” so that the destruction of the monarchy is here predicted (cf. Hos 10:15).
